entries.name: Q-learning
entries.definition: A model-free reinforcement-learning method that incrementally updates action-value estimates toward an observed reward plus the discounted maximum estimated value of the next state’s actions.
entries.identity_notes: The record captures one-step Q-learning through the original finite tabular formulation and its explicitly conditional convergence statement. It is distinct from a learned Q table, a generic reinforcement-learning task, the complete deep Q-network procedure with replay and target networks, and Ant-Q’s edge-based constructive search. Maximizing the next-state estimate distinguishes its target from simply evaluating the next action chosen by the behavior policy. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 295 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 57 and 57 lines respectively. Text hits were prior candidate leads and neighboring-method mentions in maintained records, saved reviews and discovery reports; they did not identify an existing record for these candidates. Six exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and six native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The state representation and sampling process must support the controlled Markov assumptions. Partial observability, changing dynamics, biased sample reuse or unvisited actions prevent importing the stated theorem unchanged. Infinite visits alone are insufficient without the learning-rate conditions.

A fixed positive learning rate violates the finite squared-sum condition; neural or other function approximation is not covered by the tabular theorem. The record does not claim all such variants fail, only that this particular guarantee does not establish their convergence.

The action-replay process in the proof is an analytical construction, not a required replay-buffer implementation. Section 4 separately discusses reusing empirical samples and warns that repeated reuse can favor the observed empirical environment. DQN’s additional machinery is not silently included.

The paper sketches undiscounted absorbing and multiple-entry extensions but does not establish every multi-step variant under the displayed theorem. Discounting, available actions, ties, terminal representation and initialization need a declared application. The proof’s full appendix was not independently audited; no benchmark claim is curated.

claims.statement: Maintain a finite table Q(x,a). On a sampled transition with current state x, action a, reward r and next state y, change only that entry to (1−alpha)*Q(x,a)+alpha*(r+gamma*max_b Q(y,b)), using the pre-update table for the target; leave other entries unchanged. Repeated samples supply rewards and next states without requiring an explicit estimated transition model. The maximum defines a greedy target even when behavior chooses an exploratory action; the update itself does not prescribe an exploration policy. In the paper’s discounted finite Markov setting, 0<gamma<1. Its theorem reports almost-sure convergence to optimal action values under bounded rewards, table representation, infinitely many samples of each state-action pair, and per-pair learning-rate sequences whose sum diverges while their squared sum converges, with 0<=alpha<1. This is an asymptotic, assumption-dependent statement, not a finite-sample stopping certificate.

entries.name: AntNet
entries.definition: A distributed adaptive routing algorithm in which forward agents sample network paths and backward agents use the measured trip times to update local traffic models and probabilistic routing tables.
entries.identity_notes: This record denotes the 1998 datagram-network AntNet formulation. Forward ants experience ordinary data queues and backward ants return with priority; the proposed later scheme using fast forward ants and estimated virtual delays is a separate extension. It is an instantiated routing method within the ant-colony approach, not all ACO algorithms, a static TSP optimizer, Q-routing, or a generic multi-agent system. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 295 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 57 and 57 lines respectively. Text hits were prior candidate leads and neighboring-method mentions in maintained records, saved reviews and discovery reports; they did not identify an existing record for these candidates. Six exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and six native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: Backward traversal requires bidirectional links; forward and reverse costs need not be equal. The simulation omits full transport-layer error, flow and congestion control, so its comparisons are not deployment guarantees or universal superiority claims.

The full-neighbor queue formula uses l_n=1−q_n/sum(q) and weights P_n+alpha*l_n. Zero queue sums and sampling from the restricted unvisited set require a declared normalization/fallback convention. The record does not silently treat the full-neighbor denominator as normalized after exclusions. Zero local traffic also needs a destination-selection convention.

Every selected completed route receives positive reinforcement in the baseline, including poorly scored routes; alternatives decrease by normalization. This is not a negative reward on the selected bad route. At r=1 other probabilities become zero, so the algebra alone supplies no permanent full-support guarantee. Positive probabilities remain positive under a finite power reweighting in exact arithmetic; that transformation suppresses rather than categorically forbids rare data routes.

The score’s interval is a deliberately rough asymmetric estimate built from adaptive statistics, not a calibrated confidence guarantee. Score parameters, window reset, zero dispersion, denominators, queue behavior and finite precision require declared conventions. Returned information can already be stale under changing traffic.

The explicit method and Figure 3 allow good-subpath updates; Section 8.3’s one-destination summary is a simplification. Relations to actor–critic, Monte Carlo and temporal-difference learning are qualified analogies in the paper; the method does not inherit tabular Q-learning convergence or require TD bootstrapping. No author simulator or empirical benchmark was run.

claims.statement: At each node maintain destination-specific next-hop probabilities summing to one and local statistics of experienced trip times, including mean, variance and a recent best time. Periodically launch forward ants with destinations biased by local data traffic. They share data queues, record visited nodes and elapsed times, and choose among unvisited neighbors whenever any are available, falling back to all neighbors only when all have already been visited. Within that eligible set, choices use routing probabilities plus an instantaneous queue-length heuristic. On revisiting a node, remove the cycle from memory; discard an ant if the cycle consumed more than half its current age. At the destination, create a backward ant carrying the recorded path; it returns along that path through higher-priority queues. At each visited node, use forward-trip elapsed times to update the destination’s local statistics and reinforce the neighbor leading forward toward that destination. Statistically good subpaths can also update their corresponding destinations. For a chosen forward neighbor f and reinforcement r in (0,1], set P_f_new=P_f+r*(1−P_f) and each other P_n_new=(1−r)*P_n. The inspected scoring scheme combines a recent-best-time ratio with a dispersion-based correction and a normalized nonlinear squash; it rewards a path relative to local traffic conditions. Data packets sample from a power-reweighted routing table, whereas forward ants also use queue heuristics. Updates are concurrent and local; measured forward times, not recursively bootstrapped estimates from downstream nodes, supply the feedback.

entries.name: Ant colony optimization
entries.definition: A metaheuristic framework for optimization in which artificial ants construct solutions using local information and communicate indirectly through shared pheromone information that is adapted from their search experience.
entries.identity_notes: The record denotes the ACO framework defined in the 1999 source, not a single fixed update equation. Ant System, ACS, MAX–MIN and AntNet are individual procedures with additional choices. The source distinguishes strict ACO instantiations from the broader class of ant-inspired algorithms, so all ant algorithms are not treated as synonyms. PBIL’s probability-vector update and other population heuristics share some ideas without becoming identical to ACO. limitations: A biological analogy is not a guarantee of optimality, exploration or prevention of stagnation. Positive feedback can concentrate search, and stochastic transitions or evaporation alone do not ensure that every feasible solution remains reachable. Constraints, candidate restrictions, zero weights and finite precision matter.

Heuristic information and daemon actions are optional or instance dependent. Source prose permits local optimization, lookahead and other extensions; these are not obligatory baseline operations. claims.statement: Represent the problem through states or solution components, feasible local moves and an objective. Artificial ants incrementally construct a solution or a component of one, maintaining private history as needed for feasibility. Their stochastic decisions use locally available pheromone information and, where configured, problem-specific heuristic information. Search experience changes the shared pheromone representation so later constructions can exploit prior discoveries. The framework schedules ant generation/activity, pheromone evaporation or forgetting, and optional globally informed daemon actions such as extra pheromone updates or local optimization. Deposits can occur during construction, after a solution is evaluated, or through the daemon; the ant’s stepwise and delayed deposit routines can both be absent when the daemon supplies deposits. A concrete algorithm must specify the representation, decision policy, update rule, scheduling and stopping criterion. Sequential or concurrent schedules are permitted by the prose; the framework does not prescribe a universal tau-power formula, inverse-cost deposit, elite rule or trail bound.

reading_notes: The first UBC AntNet PDF had unusable glyph encoding. The alternative public arXiv archival PDF had split words and corrupt numeric glyphs; declared method pages were OCR-read and critical equations checked visually. OCR extraction of page34 was performed but it was not read.

Q-learning equation1 updates only the observed state/action and uses the maximum next-state action value; other entries are unchanged. Theorem equation3 requires bounded rewards, finite discrete Markov state/action spaces, discounted setting, infinitely many visits and per-pair stepsizes with divergent sum and finite squared sum. Image shows 0<=alpha<1. Proof details in pages5–6 and9–14 were not independently audited. Sections4 pages7–8 qualify undiscounted absorbing extensions, replay bias and multi-step limitations.

ACO is a metaheuristic/framework synthesized from implementations, distinct from Ant System and from every ant-inspired algorithm. Daemon actions are optional; ant stepwise and delayed deposits may be absent if daemon deposits occur. Heuristics and schedules are implementation dependent. Figure3 caption mentions in_parallel although code uses schedule_activities; prose permits sequential or parallel scheduling. Source discussion does not justify universal performance or stagnation prevention. Its evolutionary-computation analogies are not imported as equivalences.

AntNet forward ants share data queues, record elapsed times and paths; returning backward ants have priority and reinforce forward-direction choices using measured forward times. Bidirectional links are required, not symmetric costs. Full destination and qualified good subpaths are updated. Source discussion8.3 simplifies to one destination entry, but explicit4.1/figure3 include good subpaths. The record should follow the explicit method and qualify that simplification.

AntNet Eq3 normalizes P+alpha*l over the full neighbor set, while prose restricts unvisited choices when possible; restricted-set renormalization and zero queue sums need an implementation convention. Every completed selected route gets nonnegative/positive reinforcement, and others decrease by normalization; this is not a negative reward for the selected bad path. Eq5–6 preserve the simplex for r in[0,1], with r1 collapsing other probabilities. Data-packet power reweighting does not make strictly positive probabilities zero in exact arithmetic.

AntNet Eq7 combines Wbest/T with interval-based correction; Eq8–9 squash and normalize s(r)/s(1). Interval is explicitly rough, asymmetric and based on exponentially estimated statistics, not calibrated statistical coverage. Exact score details and degenerate denominators need declared conventions. The original method is not the future high-priority-forward-ant variant, nor Q-routing/TD bootstrapping.

native_neighbors.definition: A family of cooperative ant-based optimization algorithms that learns shared edge desirabilities using Q-learning-inspired next-state estimates and delayed reinforcement from completed solutions.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record denotes the Ant-Q family through its traveling-salesman formulations, especially pseudo-random-proportional construction and best-tour reinforcement. Its next-state estimate distinguishes the nondegenerate Ant-Q update from the selected ACS rule targeting a constant tau0. The authors relate Ant System to the broader family; that relationship does not make every Ant-Q configuration identical to Ant System. This is an algorithm-family concept, not a trained value function or a proof of Q-learning equivalence. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 291 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 61 and 71 lines respectively. Text hits were prior candidate leads, citations to a reused Ant System source, neighboring mechanism distinctions, saved review/report material, and unrelated PBIL strings in ignored HOGENOM prefix-map URLs. Eight exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and five native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The eligible action set depends on an ant’s visited-city history, while AQ is shared per edge. City identity alone is therefore not a complete Markov state for tour feasibility. The 1995 conclusion treats transfer of Q-learning theory as future work; standard Q-learning convergence is not an established Ant-Q guarantee here.

The 1995 generic diagram loops over edges to compute delayed reinforcement and gives an incompletely specified final update domain; its repeat jump omits explicit state reset and its terminal local maximum needs a convention. The 1996 method makes best-tour-only global updates and per-tour reset explicit but references its update equation without restating the earlier zero-next-state convention. The record preserves these version details instead of claiming a fully executable common pseudocode.

The pseudo-random, pseudo-random-proportional and random-proportional construction rules are distinct members. Positive trails alone do not ensure exploration when q0=1, candidates are excluded or weights vanish. Empty eligible sets, zero distances, ties, repeated edge updates and numerical underflow require explicit handling.

The learned edge values guide stochastic search rather than certify globally optimal tours. Heuristic choice, parameters, number of ants, update ordering and stopping affect results. Neither the paper’s observed noncollapse nor its TSP/ATSP comparisons is asserted as a universal guarantee.

claims.statement: Maintain shared positive AQ(r,s) edge values, a heuristic HE(r,s) such as inverse positive distance, and each ant’s set J of unvisited cities. In the pseudo-random-proportional variant, draw q uniformly in [0,1]: for q<=q0 choose an eligible edge maximizing AQ^delta*HE^beta, otherwise sample with probabilities proportional to those weights over eligible cities. While constructing tours, the displayed update is AQ(r,s)_new=(1−alpha)*AQ(r,s)+alpha*(DeltaAQ(r,s)+gamma*max_{z in J(s)} AQ(s,z)); immediate DeltaAQ is zero in the inspected variants. After completing tours, delayed reinforcement is W/L_best on edges of a selected best tour and zero elsewhere. The paper studies both iteration-best and best-so-far choices and selects iteration-best for most subsequent experiments. In the 1995 Figure1 delayed phase, the next-state term is explicitly declared zero, so the per-edge update where applied reduces to (1−alpha)*AQ+alpha*DeltaAQ. The 1996 presentation explicitly restricts that global phase to the iteration-best tour and resets per-tour ant state each iteration. These are source-scoped formulations; terminal handling and the exact edge-update schedule must be declared when implementing a concrete member.

native_neighbors.name: Ant System
native_neighbors.definition: A constructive combinatorial optimization method in which artificial ants sample solution components using shared pheromone trails and problem-specific heuristic information, then modify those trails through reinforcement and evaporation.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record covers Ant System through its canonical ant-cycle traveling-salesman formulation. Ant-density and ant-quantity are named variants in the same source; their per-step deposits are not substituted for the ant-cycle update. Ant System is a specific predecessor within ant-colony optimization, not an alias for every later ant algorithm. Its visited-city list enforces tour feasibility and is not the generic Tabu Search framework. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 288 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 10 and 10 lines respectively. Every text hit was a prior candidate lead. limitations: The displayed inverse-distance and inverse-tour-length expressions require positive finite distances and tour lengths. Probability normalization needs finite nonnegative weights with a positive total. Zero pheromone, underflow or infeasible candidates require explicit handling.

Setting alpha=0 removes pheromone dependence; it leaves heuristic-weighted random selection, not a deterministic nearest-neighbor rule. Equal initial pheromone likewise does not imply uniform selection when heuristic values differ.

All-ant reinforcement can concentrate search prematurely. A best-so-far archive is not an optimality certificate; the source’s empirical convergence discussion does not establish a general finite-budget optimum. definition_evidence.locator: Sections II–III, PDF pp.5–8, Equations 1–4 and ant-cycle pseudocode; discussion and conclusions, PDF pp.22–24

claims.statement: In the inspected positive-distance traveling-salesman formulation, place m ants at starting cities and initialize pheromone trails. An ant at city i samples an unvisited city j with probability proportional to tau_ij^alpha * eta_ij^beta, where eta_ij=1/d_ij; normalize over the currently unvisited cities. Each ant stores its visited cities and returns to its start after visiting every city. After all tours are complete, the ant-cycle rule updates every trail as tau_ij_new=rho*tau_ij+sum_k delta_tau_ij_k, with delta_tau_ij_k=Q/L_k if ant k used that edge and zero otherwise. Here rho is retention, 1−rho is evaporation, and L_k is the completed tour length. Reset tour-specific visited lists and deposit accumulators for the next iteration while retaining the best tour found. Ant-density instead deposits a constant Q per traversed edge at each step; ant-quantity deposits Q/d_ij per step. Those variants do not use the ant-cycle complete-tour deposit.

native_neighbors.name: Ant Colony System
native_neighbors.definition: An ant-colony optimization algorithm that combines a greedy-or-proportional construction rule, local pheromone updates during construction, and global pheromone updates restricted to a selected best tour.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: The selected baseline is the paper’s global-best ACS with local interpolation toward the initial trail tau0. It is distinct from Ant System’s all-ant deposits, MAX–MIN trail clipping, and the Ant-Q variant whose local target uses a discounted maximum future trail. Iteration-best reinforcement and ACS with local search are explicitly described variants, not silently incorporated into the baseline. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 288 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 10 and 10 lines respectively. Every text hit was a prior candidate lead. Six exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and five native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The local update moves a trail toward tau0: it decreases a trail only when that trail exceeds tau0, increases it below tau0, and leaves equality unchanged. It is not unconditional evaporation. At q0=1 the displayed decision uses only maximization, apart from tie handling, so positive trails alone do not supply probabilistic exploration.

There is a source presentation ambiguity: Equation 4 defines zero deposit off the best tour, while Section III explicitly restricts the global update to best-tour edges. Appendix A’s global loop uses stale ant-indexed endpoints inside a generic edge loop, and its repeat jump does not explicitly reset all tour state. The record follows the main-text scope and supplies the necessary state-reset qualification; it does not claim the appendix is directly executable or that an official erratum was checked.

Random initial cities, heuristic powers, q0, alpha, rho and tau0 are configuration choices. Repeated local updates and their ordering affect trails; independent construction of entire tours is not an equivalent schedule. Zero distances, zero denominators, constraints and numerical underflow need handling.

The paper’s task-specific comparisons, optional local search and qualitative improvement claims do not establish universal superiority or finite-run global optimality. Ant-Q’s reinforcement-learning connection does not make the selected tau0 rule a Bellman update.

claims.statement: For a traveling-salesman tour, at each construction decision draw q uniformly in [0,1]. If q<=q0, choose an unvisited city maximizing tau_ij*eta_ij^beta; otherwise sample proportionally to those same weights over the unvisited set. Apply the selected local rule tau_ij_new=(1−rho)*tau_ij+rho*tau0 to traversed edges during construction. After all tours finish, update edges belonging to the shortest tour found so far with tau_ij_new=(1−alpha)*tau_ij+alpha/L_best. The scope of this global step follows Section III’s explicit best-tour-edge restriction; edges outside that tour do not undergo this global update. Figure 3 organizes construction into steps. Appendix A has all ants choose a step before its local-update loop, so sequential whole-tour construction is not assumed. Retain the best-so-far tour and reset per-tour feasibility state before the next iteration. Parameter settings, tie handling and repeated updates to an edge must be declared for an executable implementation.

native_neighbors.name: MAX–MIN Ant System
native_neighbors.definition: An ant-colony optimization algorithm that reinforces solution components from a single selected best ant per iteration, constrains pheromone trails between lower and upper limits, and initializes trails high to encourage early exploration.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record denotes MAX–MIN Ant System as described in the inspected 1999 author preprint associated with the 2000 journal article. It retains the defining bounded-trail and single-best reinforcement mechanism. Iteration-best, global-best and mixed schedules are specified choices; local search, candidate lists and pheromone smoothing are optional configurations. It is not the unbounded all-ant Ant System update or the selected ACS greedy/local-update rule. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 288 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 10 and 10 lines respectively. Every text hit was a prior candidate lead. limitations: Positive lower trails provide nonzero probabilities only for choices that remain eligible and have positive finite heuristic weights with a finite positive normalizer. The paper’s optional nearest-neighbor candidate lists exclude otherwise feasible choices, and its fallback is deterministic maximization; positive bounds therefore do not prove full tour support for that implementation.

The p_best lower-limit heuristic assumes the simplified TSP branching model, alpha=1 and negligible heuristic differences; changing the pheromone exponent changes the displayed probability relation. Choosing p_best=1 yields tau_min=0 in the displayed formula, which does not satisfy a strict positive-bound premise. Small n, changing branch counts and numerical underflow require additional configuration decisions.

The geometric-series argument bounds a recurrence under a maximum deposit. That argument alone does not establish that every changing trail sequence has a limit, nor that a finite run reaches the global optimum. The source’s trail-bound notion of convergence must not be equated with optimality or all ants taking the same tour.

Equal high pheromone does not imply uniform construction when heuristic weights differ. Best-so-far reinforcement, iteration-best mixing, candidate lists, local search, smoothing and restart rules affect behavior and must be declared. The reported TSP/QAP comparisons are not reproduced and no universal performance guarantee is asserted.

definition_evidence.locator: Sections 2.3 and 4.1–4.3, PDF pp.5–6 and 13–18, Equations 2–11 (lower-limit heuristic in Equations 8–11); optional variants, PDF pp.21–23; conclusions, PDF pp.32–34

claims.statement: Construct solutions by choosing feasible components with probabilities proportional to tau^alpha*eta^beta, as in Ant System. For positive-cost minimization, select one iteration-best or best-so-far solution according to the declared reinforcement schedule. Evaporate every trail using retention rho and add 1/f(best) only to components of that selected solution, with zero deposit elsewhere. Clip the resulting trails to [tau_min,tau_max] after each iteration. The source initializes trails at a high value that is brought to the upper limit; this preserves initial exploration pressure relative to low trails. Its upper-limit estimate is tau_max=1/((1−rho)*f(best_so_far)), updated when the best cost improves. For the source’s TSP lower-limit heuristic, n is the number of cities and avg=n/2 approximates the number of choices at each step. The displayed formula uses unit pheromone exponent alpha=1, equal decision probabilities and negligible heuristic differences: with p_dec=p_best^(1/n), tau_min=tau_max*(1−p_dec)/((avg−1)*p_dec), capped at tau_max if larger. This is an approximate configuration rule, not the exact probability of reconstructing a real tour. Positive limits, 0<=rho<1, a valid denominator and declared handling of boundary parameters are required for this account.

native_neighbors.name: Population-based incremental learning
native_neighbors.definition: An optimization method that samples candidate solutions from a probability-vector representation and incrementally moves that representation toward high-evaluation sampled solutions, with probability-vector mutation in its basic formulation.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: The inspected baseline uses independent Bernoulli coordinates for fixed-length binary solutions and moves toward the current generation’s single best sample. Multiple-positive and negative-example updates are explicit extensions. It is not continual learning, supervised classification, direct crossover of persistent chromosomes, or the general cross-entropy optimization framework. A single-elite Bernoulli CE fit with smoothing can coincide with the PBIL attraction step; that shared subcase does not establish equivalence of the full named procedures. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 291 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 61 and 71 lines respectively. Text hits were prior candidate leads, citations to a reused Ant System source, neighboring mechanism distinctions, saved review/report material, and unrelated PBIL strings in ignored HOGENOM prefix-map URLs. Eight exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and five native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The product of coordinate marginals cannot represent general dependencies between bits or arbitrary mixtures of dissimilar good solutions. Different populations can have the same marginals; representation and encoding affect the search.

A high learning rate can concentrate probabilities prematurely; a very low rate can make adaptation slow. With interior probabilities and 0<LR<1, a finite attraction step stays interior in exact arithmetic, but this does not guarantee lasting exploration or a finite-budget global optimum. Mutation events can be absent, and floating-point probabilities can collapse.

Probability-vector mutation is not a bit flip of every sampled chromosome and is not guaranteed to increase diversity on each event: a move toward an already favored endpoint can increase concentration. Mutation toward .5 is discussed separately as a future alternative.

Selection of the current-generation winner depends on objective ordering, whereas tie handling, objective direction, noise, population size and mutation randomization remain configuration choices. A preserved output archive does not force that archived vector into future samples. The report’s comparative results are not universal performance guarantees.

claims.statement: Initialize each binary-coordinate probability P_i to .5. At each generation, independently sample a population of binary vectors according to P, evaluate them and choose a sample x_best with the highest objective value in that generation. Update each coordinate P_i_new=(1−LR)*P_i+LR*x_best_i. Then, with a configured mutation probability per coordinate, shift that probability toward a randomly chosen binary endpoint b using P_i_new=(1−MUT_SHIFT)*P_i+MUT_SHIFT*b. Repeat for the selected budget or stopping rule. For these convex-update interpretations, LR and MUT_SHIFT lie in [0,1]. Maintain the highest-evaluation solution vectors separately for return, as the Figure4 caption recommends. The baseline updates its distribution toward the current-generation winner, not automatically the best-so-far archive. Injecting the archived best into later populations, moving toward several winners, or learning away from differing bits of poor samples are separately described extensions.
